query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pack aluminizing treatment will enhance the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr by forming a continuous, thin (approximately 1–2 μm) diffusion aluminide layer that, upon subsequent oxidation during service at high temperatures (800–1000 °C), converts to an adherent Al₂O₃ scale, thereby retarding oxygen ingress and pesting without degrading the alloy’s established room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Subject the cast sample to a pack aluminizing process using an aluminum-rich powder pack, heating at approximately 900 °C for a duration (e.g., 4 hours) to allow controlled diffusion of aluminum into the surface.
generation.conditions: Post-treatment service conditions: prolonged exposure in air at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C for at least 5 hours; strain rates in the range 10⁻⁴ – 10⁻² s⁻¹ during mechanical testing to simulate high-temperature loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a uniform, continuous, and thin diffusion aluminide layer that subsequently oxidizes to a dense, adherent Al₂O₃ scale acting as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: During the pack aluminizing treatment, aluminum diffuses into the near-surface region, forming an aluminide interlayer. Upon exposure to oxidizing conditions at high temperature, this layer preferentially oxidizes to Al₂O₃, which is thermodynamically stable, slow-growing, and has low oxygen permeability. This barrier prevents further oxygen penetration, thus mitigating the pesting phenomenon without compromising the bulk microstructure and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the pack-aluminized sample will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation weight gain and reduced surface degradation (pesting) during 5-hour exposures at 800–1000 °C, while tensile ductility and yield strength at room temperature and at elevated temperatures remain within the original performance range (approximately 8–16% ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength, with negligible degradation).
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which shows inadequate oxygen resistance (evidenced by pesting) during high-temperature exposure in air.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to hold for exposures in air up to around 1000 °C and durations of at least 5 hours. The coating must remain intact under service conditions (cyclic thermal/mechanical loads) and should be limited to a thin surface layer to avoid compromising bulk properties.
generation.uncertainty: Potential uncertainties include the uniformity and adhesion of the aluminide coating, the possibility of scale spallation under thermal cycling or mechanical loading, and the sensitivity of the diffusion process to slight variations in processing parameters. The effect on long-term mechanical performance under cyclic or extended high-temperature exposures also requires validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples—one set subjected to the optimized pack aluminizing treatment and an untreated control set. Expose both sets to isothermal air conditions at 900 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform microstructural and weight-gain analyses to assess the extent of oxidation and pesting. Additionally, conduct room-temperature and high-temperature tensile tests to evaluate the mechanical performance.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain and oxide scale thickness (by gravimetric analysis and microscopy)
Surface microstructure and adherence of the oxide scale (via SEM/EDS)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pack-aluminized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >30% improvement) in oxidation damage (lower weight gain, no pesting) compared to the untreated controls, or if the mechanical performance (ductility and yield strength) degrades by more than 10–15% relative to the baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. HfNbTaTiZr is a high-entropy alloy, and according to a calculated VEC value of 4.4, it has a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure. The alloy was developed by mechanical alloying from high-purity metallic powders in a Pulverisette 6 classic line planetary ball mill (Fritsch®, Idar-Oberstein, Germany) with a stainless steel vial and grinding media. Due to the powder reactivity, handling and alloying were performed under an argon atmosphere. To avoid the welding of the alloy to the vial and balls and to reduce the oxidation and contamination of powders, n-heptane was used as a control process agent (PCA). Milling parameters were selected after multiple trials to ensure that the powders were not overheating. A mixture of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr high-purity powders was milled for 60 h, and samples were taken at different time intervals to evaluate the alloying degree. After the alloying process, the particle size was reduced, and a good homogeneity was obtained. With further processing represented by sintering and deposition, the alloying degree was increased. papers.title: Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr (and subtraction variants such as HfNbTaTiZr) refractory high‐entropy alloys
papers.approach: Systematic subtraction method to analyze elemental contributions; characterization of microstructure and mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures with discussion on further modifications including composition tweaks and anti‐oxidation coatings.
papers.findings: Found that while the equiatomic alloy exhibits strong room‐ and high-temperature performance, its composition leaves it vulnerable to oxidation; the authors note that further modification via compositional changes and/or anti‐oxidation coatings is required for high‐temperature applications.
papers.mechanism: Oxygen attacks the alloy due to inadequate oxidation resistance; a protective barrier (via either coating or selective alloying) is suggested to hinder oxygen ingress without compromising the high strength and ductility.

papers.title: New HfNbTaTiZr High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Produced by Electrospark Deposition with High Corrosion Resistance.
papers.system: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy as a coating material
papers.approach: Used electrospark deposition to produce a coating of HfNbTaTiZr on substrates and evaluated its corrosion (and by proxy, oxidation) resistance.
papers.findings: The resultant coatings exhibited high corrosion resistance that implies improved oxidation protection without significantly altering the inherent mechanical properties of the underlying alloy.
papers.mechanism: The electrospark process produces a coating with a dense microstructure that can support the formation of protective oxides; this barrier retards further oxygen penetration under high-temperature conditions.

papers.title: Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film.
papers.approach: Subjected the amorphous HEA film to thermal shock (annealing at 800 °C for 1 h) to study its oxidation behavior.
papers.findings: After annealing, a dense composite oxide layer (ZrTiO4) formed on the film’s surface which effectively prevented further oxidation; the film retained excellent tribocorrosion resistance.
papers.mechanism: Protective composite oxide layer formation acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance even under high-temperature environments.

established: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits excellent room- and high-temperature mechanical performance but suffers from poor oxygen resistance.
Prior studies in related non-equiatomic alloys have demonstrated that modifications—either via composition or surface treatments—can inhibit pesting/oxidation at high temperatures.

approaches_tried.outcome: Improved mechanical properties though oxidation resistance was not directly established; related non-equiatomic variants have shown better oxidation behavior in specific tests (e.g., 5 h exposure at 800 °C).

approaches_tried.approach: Application of protective coatings (e.g., via electrospark deposition)
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced coatings with high corrosion resistance suggestive of improved oxidation protection without detriment to mechanical performance.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal shock treatment to enable in situ formation of protective oxide layers
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of a dense composite oxide (ZrTiO4) layer that served as an effective oxidation barrier.

mechanisms: Formation of protective oxide scales (e.g., Al2O3, ZrTiO4) can hinder oxygen diffusion into the alloy substrate.
Dense coatings produced through electrospark deposition or thermal treatments provide a physical barrier against oxidative attack.
Reactive element effects: minor additions (e.g., Al when optimized) can promote the formation of thermodynamically stable oxides that improve oxygen resistance.
disagreements: While some studies propose compositional adjustments as a solution, others are investigating external coatings; the optimal route for the equiatomic composition without compromising mechanical performance remains debated.
open_questions: Can a single, surface-targeted intervention (such as a protective coating) sufficiently improve oxygen resistance in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without altering its superior mechanical properties?
What is the optimal protective scale (e.g., composition, thickness, adherence) for long-term high-temperature exposure in air?
How might controlled minor elemental additions (e.g., a low level of Al) compare with surface coatings in providing oxidation resistance for the equiatomic alloy?
opportunities: Investigate the application of thin, externally applied anti-oxidation coatings (for example, aluminide or other reactive-element-based coatings) on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to form a protective oxide barrier.
Pursue systematic thermal treatments that encourage in situ formation of a continuous, dense oxide (analogous to the ZrTiO4 formation reported in HEA films) on the alloy surface.

Evaluate a controlled, minor dopant addition (such as Al) as a single composition modification that might promote the formation of a protective Al2O3 scale while preserving the mechanical performance.
Develop a combined study that compares surface coating versus minor alloying interventions under identical high-temperature oxidation conditions to identify the most effective single intervention.

directions.direction: Introduce a minor bulk alloying addition of aluminum to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to promote the in situ formation of a protective Al₂O₃ scale during high‐temperature exposure.
directions.assessment: This route directly improves oxidation resistance through reactive element effects by forming a thermodynamically stable alumina barrier. However, even slight changes in bulk composition risk altering the established room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of the equiatomic alloy.

directions.direction: Apply a controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment that induces the formation of an in situ, dense composite oxide (e.g., ZrTiO₄ or similar) on the surface.
directions.assessment: This approach leverages controlled annealing to create a protective oxide layer. While attractive because it does not change the composition, the reliability and uniformity of the in situ scale, as well as its long-term adhesion under cyclic or prolonged exposure, remain uncertain.

directions.direction: Utilize laser surface alloying with an aluminum-rich precursor to modify only the near-surface composition, fostering the formation of a protective alumina scale.
directions.assessment: This intervention targets only the surface without affecting the bulk. It is conceptually sound based on reactive element strategies; however, process complexity and potential localized thermal effects need careful evaluation.

directions.direction: Implement an electrospark deposition (ESD) process to deposit a thin, dense aluminide coating (pre-alloyed HfNbTaTiZr with added aluminum) onto the cast substrate.
directions.assessment: Electrospark deposition has been used successfully to produce corrosion‐resistant coatings on similar alloys. This method can form a dense coating that will oxidize to Al₂O₃, offering protection while minimally impacting the bulk mechanical properties. Process control and scale adhesion are critical but are well within current technological capabilities.

directions.direction: Perform a pack aluminizing treatment, where the cast alloy is exposed to an aluminum-rich powder pack at elevated temperatures to form a diffusion aluminide layer that then oxidizes to a protective alumina scale.
directions.assessment: Pack aluminizing is a well-established method for forming protective alumina scales on high-temperature alloys. It avoids bulk compositional changes and is directly focused on enhancing oxidation resistance. The process parameters (temperature, duration, pack composition) can be optimized to obtain a thin (~1–2 μm), adherent coating without compromising the alloy’s mechanical integrity.

choice.why: Pack aluminizing directly addresses the oxygen resistance issue by forming an adherent, dense aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) scale on the surface, a well‐known protective barrier that retards oxygen ingress. This single surface intervention avoids altering the bulk equiatomic composition—thereby preserving the useful room- and high-temperature mechanical properties—and is supported by previous studies showing that external coatings can effectively inhibit oxidation (e.g., PMC8348113 and PMC10456374).
